# Kāmanītajātaka (Ja 228)

**ID:** Ja 228
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Kāmanītajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Brahmin Named Desire-Led
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja228
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul1.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kāmanītajātaka* (Ja 228) is a story of the Buddha's previous lives set at Jetavana, delivered by the Buddha regarding a brahmin named Kāmanīta [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879]. The commentary observes that the full background details for both the present and past circumstances of the narrative are explained in the Twelfth Book (*Dvādasanipāta*) under the *Kāmajātaka* [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879]. The character's name derives from the Pali noun *kāma* ("sense pleasure" or "desire") and translates literally as "Desire-Led" [SuttaCentral; Gjellerup 1999].

In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta is born as the king of the gods, Sakka [Anandajoti 2010; Jetjiravat; Fausböll 1879]. Taking the guise of a young brahmin, he visits a ruler plagued by insatiable greed, lust, and craving for wealth, and speaks of conquering three prosperous kingdoms [Anandajoti 2010; Jetjiravat; UNDV Conference Volume 2009]. Yearning intensely to acquire these lands, the king is overcome by physical illness brought on by mental obsession and stress [Jetjiravat; UNDV Conference Volume 2009]. He is brought to his senses by the admonition that bodily needs are inherently finite whereas desires are endless: even if he conquered four kingdoms, he could never wear four garments, lie upon four royal beds, or consume meals from four dishes at once [UNDV Conference Volume 2009]. After delivering this instruction, Sakka establishes the king in moral virtue (*sīla*) before departing for the deva realm [Fausböll 1879]. In the story's resolution (*samodhāna*), the Buddha reveals that the greedy king was reborn as the brahmin Kāmanīta, while Sakka was the Bodhisatta [Fausböll 1879].

Neither SuttaCentral nor DharmaNexus records any external cross-language parallels in Chinese, Sanskrit, or Tibetan [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. However, DharmaNexus identifies internal Pali text reuse spanning six segments (461 characters) shared directly with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Dutiyo bhāgo), particularly covering the narrative verses and commentary (§1.4–2.4) [DharmaNexus].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Text reuse within the Pali corpus (DharmaNexus): Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā (Dutiyo bhāgo) (Atk S0513a2) (§1.4–2.4 ↔ §1373–1374)

**Sources**

- [SuttaCentral] SuttaCentral record for ja228 — Supplied title, canonical reference, introductory blurb linking to the Kāmajātaka, and confirmed absence of external parallels.
- [DharmaNexus] DharmaNexus text-reuse database — Provided automated internal reuse data with the Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā and confirmed the lack of cross-language matches.
- [Fausböll 1879] V. Fausböll, The Jātaka together with Its Commentary, Vol. 2 (1879) — Supplied the Pali introductory framework, connection to the Dvādasanipāta, and the samodhāna identifying the past lives.
- [Anandajoti 2010] Anandajoti Bhikkhu, Buddhist Wisdom Verses: 551 Verses from the Canon (2010) — Summarized the narrative core of Sakka disguising himself to cure the king's greed.
- [Jetjiravat] P. Jetjiravat, Direct Causal Link Between Illness and Kamma: A Buddhist Perspective — Described the king's physical illness as rooted in mental disease and insatiable craving.
- [UNDV Conference Volume 2009] UNDV Conference Volume: Buddhist Approach to Environmental Crisis (2009) — Noted the lesson on limited physical needs versus endless desires using the example of four robes, beds, and dishes.
- [Gjellerup 1999] Karl Gjellerup, Pilgrim Kamanita: A Legendary Romance (ed./repr. 1999) — Provided the etymology of the name Kāmanīta from kāma and its occurrence at Ja 228.
